title: Computer History Museum Recovers Rare UNIX History
transcriptText:
I'm Al Caso, the Robert N. Miner
software curator. I've been at the
Computer History Museum since 2006 and
before that I was at Apple Computer for
20 years.
Um, primarily the responsibility of the
software curator is the collection and
management of the software assets that
have been accumulated during the history
of the museum and the acquisitions that
happened before that. As the software
curator, I'm responsible for
building the collection and matching it
up with the hardware artifacts that we
have along with accumulating new
information.
And part of that job is recovering the
actual software from the containers like
mag tapes and disc packs and all the
different kinds of things that we have,
which is what uh I do here in the
software preservation lab. Once we get
the material off of the original
container, we put it into a form that
can be stored in the CHM digital
repository
and be made available through the CHM
website. In addition to people that have
original old hardware, there are people
in the last 10 or 20 years that have
written emulation software that can run
the software that we've collected. So
we're going to be trying to make all of
that information available to them as
well. The actual workflow for recovering
the data varies depending on the type of
media. Magnetic tape is particularly
difficult to deal with because in the
last you know 40 50 years the the
magnetic tape itself hasn't aged very
well. So part of the process of the big
part of the process of media recovery of
magnetic tape is trying to get that
binder back into a stable enough
condition where it doesn't um come off
of the surface of the tape while you're
reading it because any changes in speed
of the tape or clogging of the head
ruins the read. Um, in preparation for
the reading of the University of Utah
tape, I have an equivalent
era magnetic tape that I've been doing
testing on to see what the condition of
that tape was.
And looking looking at that, it it
should be relatively straightforward.
I'm Len Chustik and I've variously been
a university professor and an
entrepreneur. In 1996, I co-founded the
Computer History Museum and I was
chairman of the board for 25 years. Um,
and then stepped down. So, my odd title
now is founding chairman emmeritus. I
was an undergraduate at the Polytenic
Institute of Brooklyn in the late 1960s
and I was privileged to be part of an
amazing project for an undergraduate to
write a compiler for a brand new
language. It was called PL1. It was
designed by IBM. It was going to be the
language used for the next 50 years,
which turned out not to be true. But we
uh as a student project decided to write
a simplified compiler for it. And we did
an amazing job at the time and it worked
well. It was used for many years by
student projects.
Uh and I left in 1970 to be a graduate
student uh in computer science at
Stanford and I brought with me this tape
of the source code of the project that
we had worked on and I kept it with me
for 50 years and it moved with me from
bedroom to attic and all the various
places that I lived. And in 2018, 50
years after we had done the project, I
decided it would be interesting to try
to recover the code from that project.
And I paid $1,000 to a professional data
recovery company to get the data off
this tape. And they totally failed. The
tape had degraded to the point where
standard tape drives couldn't read the
data anymore. there was some data on the
tape and I was convinced there was some
way to get that data out, but you
couldn't use a standard tape drive to do
it. So, I decided to start on a project
to look at the analog information on the
tape, not try to record or read the
digital information.
You know, we live in this fantasy world
where we think that computers work on
binary in zeros and ones, but that's
really a fiction. The world is analog
and we interpret some of the analog
information as bits as digital
information. So for electronics if a
voltage is less than8 volts we decide
it's a zero. If it's greater than 2
volts we decide it's a one. If it's in
between those two values it's
indeterminate but there is still some
information there. So I decided the way
to do this was to recover this tape was
to look at the analog information on the
tape and then in software try to figure
out what the bits were. So I embarked on
this project. I started off by designing
my own tape transport and my own
electronics to read the analog
information on the tape and was having a
hard time with that project and was
commiserating with Al Caso, the Computer
History Museum software curator, and he
came up with this brilliant idea of
using a standard tape drive, having it
read the tape, but tapping into the
electronics of the tape drive at the
point where it just has recovered the
anal analog information and hasn't yet
decoded the bits, the zeros and the
ones. And we would record that analog
information and feed that into a program
to reconstruct the data. And that's what
I did. It's surprising to me that the
original CC code for Unix has been lost
and no one has it. And it's exciting
that the tape has been recently
discovered and we are awaiting today the
arrival of the tape and we're going to
put it through this tape recovery
process using retape to try to recover
the original source code from the first
C version of Unix. That's historically
very important. The first step is going
to be uh just a visual inspection. Uh,
from looking at the picture, it it looks
like the reel is in is physically in
good shape.
Um, I'll put it on uh I have a small um
Graham magnetic tape conditioner that um
for for this operation normally what
what it would do is there's a sapphire
blade that goes across the surface the
the recording surface of the tape and
you know
they're they're called tape scrapers is
they they'll clean off any any debris.
And then there's a little vacuum system
that that pulls it away from the tape.
For for this, I'm going to put a piece
of cloth over the the sapphire blade and
have a u a cloth on the input side of
the path with a little bit of
cyclomethone,
which is a um uh it's used in the
cosmetics industry. It's a light
silicone lubricant
and uh kind of kind of condition the
surface of the tape with that. Then make
a make a pass through the t through the
tape in in the forward direction. Rewind
it and
u that should all be all that's
necessary. So from there
u I'll put it on the tape the tape
drive. Uh I have all the software set up
for digitizing it. I use a a
Pro 16
uh analog 16 channel analog digital
converter
um hooked up to um their data
acquisition program.
I I'm I suspect that it's going to be an
800 BPI tape. So that means there's
going to be 800
flux transitions
across the surf surface of the tape
every every inch. The tape moves at 50
inches per second. So that's going to be
40,000 flux transitions
and I'll be running the digitizer at
center 750,000
samples per second. So it's it's you
know over 10 times over sampling.
Then from there,
I'll uh translate
the data from the analog to digital
converter into the form that Len needs
for his program. We'll run read tape
across it and hopefully we'll we'll get
correct data back out of that.
>> So, my name is Talia Archeald. I'm a PhD
student at the University of Utah. I
just started last semester and um I do
work in compiler verification. So this
kind of area really interests me and it
was complete chance. I was working in
the lab one day and I get this message
from the Unix Heritage Society titled
Unix V4 tape found. And I read a message
to our grad school Slack channel random
saying just a blurb the Unix V4 tape was
found. I didn't know where. And uh I
wrote this is the only one known in the
world. None of the others survived. It
was the first kernel written in C. Press
send. And then a minute later, Rob
Richie replies. He says, "Oh yeah, we
found it. That was my team." So this
message was from Rob Pike. He was an old
oldtime Bell Labs guy now known for
creating the Go programming language.
And so I thought, "Oh, this is of course
this is something Rob Pike would care
about. This is somewhere in the world."
And um I had no idea. It was very neat
to find out that I was just down the
hall from where it was found, where it
was used. Then I bring my whole lab over
to his office and we're all just
crowding around the tape looking. Oh,
whoa. I'm holding a piece. I'm holding a
piece of 51y old history. And so we all
got photos with it and uh says Unix V4
disc on it. It's got this handwritten
label saying more about it. So, we were
all very excited.
>> I'm John Durig from the University of
Utah. Uh my group is the research or is
the flux research group. We uh do a lot
of uh research in networking. So, this
this tape was very important. It wasn't,
you know, it's it's important in a
systems research sense. We do systems
research, but in, you know, in some
ways, this this tape doesn't really
connect with what we do except that Jay
happened to have a copy of it. The
founder of our group is Jayla Pro. His
he was a pretty foundational person in
computer science. He did a lot of
research and he worked at the U for many
years. He passed away in 2008. So at the
time we had already boxed up a lot of
his uh effects because we were doing a
move and he didn't live to see his new
office where he was going to move all
the stuff to. So in that in the time
just after he passed away, we just put
all of these, you know, all all of these
old office documents, you know, thing
old expense reports and old, you know,
things from his file cabinet. We put it
all into a storage room and we didn't
look at it for another, you know, 20
years. So one of our research
associates, Alex Marik, he has been
going through the old boxes of Jay's
effects and getting rid of what we don't
need. While he was doing that, at one
point, you know, he kind of shouted out
to us, "Hey, I found this cool thing."
And uh we we you know, me and my
colleagues, we all kind of looked and
over this old mag tape. Um you know,
some of us are old enough to remember
actually using mag tapes, but you know,
many of us are are too young. And so, uh
it just seemed like a neat piece of
incidental history. We liked we thought
it was a cool artifact. Uh, and after
after ooing and aing over a bit, I was
like, wait, you know, is there is Unix
is there a copy of the Unix source? Is
does this even exist? And uh so I went
back to my computer and started
searching. I was like, "Oh, yeah,
there's plenty of copies of Unix, but
what version is it?" And uh you know,
Alex looked, it says it's version 4. It
turns out there's no accident copy of
version 4, or rather there wasn't an
accident copy of version four. And we
were uh we were very excited to see
that. You know, having said that, you
know, that's just the contents of the
label. That's not the contents of the
tape. So, uh, we, you know, we were
tried to be very cautious, tamp down our
expectations, kind of going back and
forth between nervousness and
excitement. And we decided to, you know,
we did some research trying to figure
out who we might contact, who might
still have a tape reader, who might uh,
take a look at this tape and see what is
actually on it. And that's when we
decided to email the computer history
museum.
>> I'm Warren B. I started the uh TUS, the
Unix heritage society back in 1994 and
I've been running it and sort of looking
after it ever since. The heritage
society, we have a mailing list and of
course anything that is vaguely unix
related sort of gets mentioned. So as
soon as someone knew there was tape in
existence, it the word got around and we
heard about it really quickly even
before it was read even before it got to
CHM. Back when Bell Labs were doing the
development, there were seven editions.
The first edition was the one that came
on the PDP11. Internally, they developed
it until the fourth edition. The fourth
edition was the first version that got
out to the public and it came after
their symposium uh presentation in 1973.
So that public announcement made people
go, "Wow, this sounds like a good thing.
Maybe we can get a copy of the tape.
Maybe we can get a copy of the system."
And also the fourth edition was the
first of the Unix systems that was
written in C. Before that they were all
in assembly. It's it's amazing to think
that they knew that they had to do it in
a high level language. They knew they
had to get away from assembly and C just
happened to be fantastic language for
doing that small close to being an
assembler but high level enough to make
it portable across different platforms.
So this tape is just another piece of
the jigsaw puzzle that paints the
picture of the progression and of Unix
and how it influenced uh the industry
once it got out in the 70s and then
became big in the 80s and 90s. Pretty
much everything that's in your pocket,
everything that hangs on your wall, if
you've got a TV, if you got an embedded
device, it's either running a clear
descendant of Unix or a clean room
rewrite of the Unix operating system.
I'm just so glad that we have you guys,
we have the other museums, that we have
people who care about protecting this
history. I think it's um the world is
now basically driven by computers and we
need to be able to bring a perspective
of where we came from, how we got to
where we are, and how that can influence
and motivate us to improve where we go
in the future.
